text:
GCLMPO opens public comment period for regional transportation project prioritization
J. D. Gould
The Gaston-Cleveland-Lincoln Metropolitan Planning Organization announced on July 24 the opening of a 15-day public comment period for input on future Regional Impact transportation projects in Gaston, Cleveland, and Lincoln Counties. The comment period is part of the process to develop the GCLMPO’s 2028-2037 Transportation Improvement Program, administered by the North Carolina Department of Transportation and referred to as Prioritization 8.0 or P8.0.
A draft list and map of proposed Regional Impact local input point assignments are available on the GCLMPO website. Residents can review these materials before submitting feedback. A separate public comment period for Division Needs projects will begin in October 2026.
According to the announcement, NCDOT has scored projects submitted by metropolitan planning organizations, rural planning organizations, and NCDOT divisions using formulas established under the Strategic Transportation Investments law. GCLMPO has been allocated 1,900 local input points each for both Regional Impact and Division Needs tiers. The STI legislation requires that all entities adhere closely to their adopted local input point methodologies when assigning points; GCLMPO’s methodology is also posted online.
The current public comment period will end on August 7, 2026. In addition to written submissions via mail, email, or fax addressed to Tori Dellinger at Gaston-Cleveland-Lincoln MPO, comments may be provided during upcoming meetings: the Technical Coordinating Committee Meeting scheduled for August 12 at 10:00 am, and the Board Meeting set for August 27 at 6:30 pm.
For further information or questions about participation in this process or accessing relevant documents, residents are encouraged to contact GCLMPO staff by phone at 704-854-6631.
Of students in Gaston County school districts taking ACT exams during the 2022-23 school year, between approximately seventeen percent and twenty-seven percent were considered ready for college across science, reading, and math sections, according to the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction.
